issues.legal_issue: A levy on residential tenanted buildings is for a public purpose and does not become an invalid property restriction merely because some owners receive incidental benefits from its proceeds.
material_facts: The legislation imposed a levy to fund a board’s work to repair or replace dangerous residential buildings and to provide accommodation for people displaced by collapses or repairs.
The levy applied to residential buildings occupied by tenants, including buildings that were sound and did not need structural repairs.

The proceeds were credited to the public account before being appropriated to the repairs and reconstruction fund, and the owner bore only part of the levy while being permitted to recover the balance from the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The levy served a public purpose of preventing building collapses and the resulting human suffering; incidental benefits to some owners did not make its purpose private or render it an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
issues.legal_principle: A taxing law must be within legislative competence, serve a public purpose, and comply with Part III of the Constitution. Under Article 19(1)(f), the public character of expenditure is judged by its purpose, not by who receives the money or whether particular taxpayers receive equivalent benefits. Incidental private benefits do not invalidate expenditure directed to a public purpose. The Court relied on Cooley on Taxation, American Jurisprudence, and Carmichael v. Southern Coal & Coke Co.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_law and levy_addresses_a_public_housing_hazard and proceeds_fund_public_prevention_or_relief and some_owners_receive_incidental_benefits

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_law: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law imposing a tax.
predicates.levy_addresses_a_public_housing_hazard: The levy is imposed to address dangers to residents arising from unsafe housing and resulting displacement or suffering.
predicates.proceeds_fund_public_prevention_or_relie: The proceeds are directed to public measures that prevent the housing danger or relieve its consequences.
predicates.some_owners_receive_incidental_benefits: Some owners may benefit from measures funded by the levy even though the levy is not directed to a private purpose.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a levy directed to public prevention or relief, incidental benefits to some owners do not prevent the levy from being treated as serving a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Classifying buildings for a housing-safety levy by residential use, tenancy, age, and construction does not violate equal protection where those distinctions relate to the danger addressed and the measure is directed to a feasible part of that problem.
material_facts: The legislation focused on existing residential buildings occupied by tenants, although dangerous buildings also existed among non-residential properties and buildings constructed later.
Government and municipal studies described recurrent collapses, the age and construction of many residential buildings, and the urgency of addressing the danger to their occupants.
The legislation divided taxable buildings into categories based on when and how they were built, and imposed the levy by reference to each building’s rateable value.

Buildings within the same category could differ in their actual condition, and some buildings did not need repairs; the levy’s primary purpose was to prevent collapses, not to ensure that every taxpayer received an individual repair benefit.
issues.conclusion: The classifications were based on intelligible differences connected to the legislation’s objectives and feasibility. Differences in actual condition or in the individual benefit received did not make the classifications discriminatory.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to taxing laws, but the legislature has substantial latitude in fiscal classification. A classification must rest on an intelligible differentia related to the law’s objective; a legislature may tax some objects without taxing all, and differences in burden or benefit within a class do not alone establish discrimination. The Court relied on K. T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala, Raja Jagannath v. State of U.P., East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Khandige Sham Bhatt v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer, State of Andhra Pradesh v. Nalla Raja Reddy, Ravi Varma v. Union of India, and Twyford Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Kerala. It held Moopil Nair and New Manek Chowk Spinning and Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad inapplicable.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_law and existing_tenant_housing_faces_a_housing_safety_hazard and the_legislature_prioritizes_a_feasible_part_of_that_hazard and classification_tracks_building_age_or_construction_or_occupancy and levy_is_assessed_by_property_value

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_law: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law imposing a tax.
predicates.existing_tenant_housing_faces_a_housing_: Existing housing occupied by tenants presents a danger to occupants from unsafe buildings or potential collapse.
predicates.the_legislature_prioritizes_a_feasible_p: The legislature chooses to address a practicable part of a wider safety problem as a priority.
predicates.classification_tracks_building_age_or_co: The tax categories distinguish buildings by characteristics such as their age, construction, or occupancy.
predicates.levy_is_assessed_by_property_value: The levy is calculated by reference to the value assigned to each property.

issues.definition: A classification for a tax addressing a housing-safety hazard is not discriminatory when it uses relevant building or occupancy characteristics to address a feasible priority, even if buildings or taxpayers within a category differ in condition or benefit.

issues.legal_issue: Exempting property groups with materially different uses, occupancy relationships, or regulatory circumstances from a housing-safety levy does not violate equal protection.
material_facts: The legislation exempted, among other groups, owner-occupied buildings, buildings used exclusively for non-residential purposes, buildings occupied on leave and licence, buildings belonging to or leased to cooperative societies, and buildings constructed after the legislation began.

The Court found that these groups differed from residential buildings occupied by tenants in relevant ways, including the application of rent controls, the rights and security of occupants, and the relationship between cooperative societies and their members.
The legislation addressed the particular circumstances associated with residential tenancies and the reluctance or inability of landlords to maintain such buildings.
issues.conclusion: The exempted groups formed distinct classes relevant to the legislation’s purpose, and the exemptions did not violate equal protection.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits different treatment where an exemption distinguishes a class on an intelligible basis connected to the law’s purpose. Buildings outside the targeted residential-tenancy problem, and those with materially different occupancy or regulatory relationships, need not be treated as equivalent to tenanted residential buildings. The Court applied the classification principles stated in Khandige Sham Bhatt v. Agricultural Income-tax Officer and its discussion of Article 14 in relation to taxing laws.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_tax_exemptio: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of an exemption from a tax.
predicates.the_levy_targets_a_defined_housing_or_oc: The tax is directed at a defined problem associated with a particular kind of housing or occupancy.
predicates.exempted_properties_have_materially_dist: The exempted properties differ from the taxed properties in their use, occupancy relationships, or applicable regulatory circumstances.

issues.definition: An exemption from a tax addressing a defined housing or occupancy problem survives an equal-protection challenge when the exempted properties have materially different relevant circumstances.
